new_statements.rule_in_words: Manda is analysed as a restricted, predictable tone language rather than a stress or word-accent language: every word surfaces with (at least one) H tone placed near the right edge — nominals H on antepenult+penult or on the penult alone (penult-only the commoner pattern), verbs toneless lexically with TAM-assigned melodic H on antepenult+penult, penult only, or stem-initial (with object marker). The only stress-like prominence is automatic penult lengthening, which falls on the penult of the phonological phrase (phrase-final word), not on every word; vowel length is otherwise non-contrastive. The author explicitly rejects Nurse's (1988) 'penultimate stress' characterization and Guthrie's 'no tone' claim (fn.29).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the source speaks only of H-tone positions (antepenult+penult vs penult) and phrase-final penult lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: Penult H often realized as falling because of penult lengthening; object markers shift some conjugations' H to stem-initial position; passive extension forces a single penult H; some exceptions to edge-placement of tone noted; Remote Future in the Matumba variety has a different pattern (Bernander 2023); fn.22: level/constructions of penult lengthening need further study. Note the text's 'final antepenultimate position of a phonological phrase' appears to be a slip for 'penultimate' — all examples (3)-(5) show lengthening of the phrase-penultimate syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Penult lengthening (prominence) is a phonological-phrase-final phenomenon: adding an object NP or the post-verbal negator lépa moves the lengthening to the end of the whole phrase while word-level H tones stay put (exx. 3-5, p.47). Tone positions are word-level. Data mainly from the northern Manda variety around Lituhi/Ludewa district; Matumba (southern) variety mentioned for some divergences.
new_statements.identity_note: Bernander's description is of Manda N.11 (glottocode mand1423, ISO mgs) as spoken on the Tanzanian shore of Lake Nyasa; his data come chiefly from the northern variety, with the southern 'Matumba' variety noted as diverging in some verb-form tone patterns (e.g. Remote Future). Not to be confused with Manda (Dravidian, mand1411) or Australian Manda (mand1469).

sources.note: Ch.5 grammar sketch, sec. 5.2.1.1 (pp.46-47) and 5.2.4 Tone (pp.54-56): Manda has no contrastive vowel length; shows 'automatic penult lengthening' giving the penult stronger prominence, but this applies phrase-finally (phonological phrase), not per word; Manda is a restricted/predictable tone language, explicitly 'not merely a stress language' and not a (word-)accent language by Hyman's criteria (H tone obligatory, demarcative near word edge, not culminative). Nominals carry H on antepenult+penult or penult only (penult-only more common; minimal pair kilólélo 'mirror' vs kilolélo 'dry season…
